# Is Stratified Class Placement More Fair for High Achievers?

**A Commentary by Dr. Jane Smith**

*Published in the Journal of Educational Policy and Practice*

---

## Introduction

Few questions in education policy provoke as much moral anxiety as stratified placement—the practice of sorting students into classes, tracks, or schools according to measured performance. Critics invoke images of gatekeeping and entrenched privilege. Defenders, myself included, must answer a sharper question than the critics usually pose: not whether stratification is comfortable, but whether it is *fair*—and to whom. In this commentary, I argue that stratified class placement, when paired with transparent admissions criteria and pathways for mobility, is not only more efficient but more fair, particularly to high-achieving students whose needs are systematically sacrificed in the name of homogeneous classrooms. I focus on two theories that structure this debate: what I will call the **selective admissions theory** and the **average drag theory**.

## The Selective Admissions Theory

The selective admissions theory holds that when placement into advanced tracks or selective programs is governed by observable performance—grades, assessments, demonstrated mastery—the resulting allocation of educational resources is meritocratic in the meaningful sense: students receive instruction matched to their readiness.

The objection immediately arises: performance is not produced in a vacuum. Students from resource-rich families enter the placement contest with tutors, test preparation, enriched home environments, and parents who know how to navigate the system. Is selective admission therefore a mechanism for laundering family advantage into institutional privilege?

This objection is serious but proves too much. Every allocation mechanism in education embeds prior advantage to some degree. Residence-based school assignment embeds it through housing markets—arguably more rigidly than test-based admission, since purchasing a home in a desirable district is far more capital-intensive than preparing for an entrance exam. Random assignment ignores both merit and need. Selective admissions at least has the virtue of rewarding *demonstrated effort and performance*, however imperfectly, and it creates an incentive structure in which family investment flows toward cultivating the child rather than merely purchasing geography.

Moreover, the relevant counterfactual is not a world without advantage but a comparison among imperfect systems. A placement system that rewards preparation and performance gives motivated students from modest backgrounds a ladder. A system that refuses to differentiate at all gives them nothing but a seat in a classroom paced for someone else.

## The Average Drag Theory

The average drag theory describes the pedagogical cost of heterogeneity. A single teacher facing a class with a wide ability dispersion must choose a target. Rational instruction aims at the middle—but the middle is a statistical fiction. The student two standard deviations above it sits through content she mastered last year; the student two standard deviations below it encounters material he cannot yet access. Both disengage, and disengagement is contagious.

The empirical signature of average drag is well documented: high-achieving students in mixed-ability classrooms show flatter growth trajectories than comparable peers in accelerated settings, and teachers in heterogeneous classrooms report systematically curtailing the depth of content. The loss falls disproportionately on students at the top of the distribution—and here is the equity point that the critics miss—*including high achievers from disadvantaged backgrounds*, who are least likely to have compensatory resources outside school. When a classroom cannot accelerate, the affluent high achiever buys acceleration privately; the poor high achiever simply stalls. Differentiated placement is thus not a luxury for the privileged. It is often the *only* acceleration mechanism available to talented students whose families cannot purchase alternatives.

The efficiency argument follows directly. Educational output is maximized when instruction is matched to readiness, and stratified placement is the most scalable technology yet devised for achieving that match. Whole-class differentiation asks one professional to be five teachers at once; stratification lets each teacher actually teach.

## Efficiency and the Fairness of Expansion

I want to be precise about what I am and am not claiming. I am not defending the rigid, early, school-wide tracking of mid-century Europe, in which a single examination at age ten fixed a child's destiny. The evidence against *that* architecture is persuasive, and mobility between tracks must be real, frequent, and administratively easy for stratification to remain fair.

What I am defending, and what I believe the evidence supports expanding, is a program of **stratified trials**: subject-specific, later-starting, continuously reassessed placement systems, piloted with rigorous evaluation. Concretely:

1. **Subject-level stratification rather than global tracking.** A student may need remediation in mathematics and belong in an accelerated literature seminar. Stratification by subject respects the reality that ability is domain-specific.
2. **Performance-based admission with multiple measures**—grades, portfolio evidence, and assessments—to reduce the noise and bias of any single gatekeeping instrument.
3. **Permeable boundaries.** Annual reassessment, clear criteria for movement between levels, and summer bridge programs that make the ladder down as real as the ladder up.
4. **Deliberate resource parity**, ensuring that lower tracks receive the strongest teachers and smallest classes, so that stratification sorts pedagogy rather than rationing quality.
5. **Sunset and evaluation provisions**, so that every stratified program must demonstrate gains—or at minimum, no harm to any group—to survive.

The fairness case for such trials rests on a simple accounting. The status quo already stratifies—by neighborhood, by parental wealth, by access to private enrichment and selective private schools. It does so opaquely and without accountability. Formal, performance-based, permeable stratification does not create differentiation; it makes differentiation *visible, contestable, and governable*. A system with explicit admissions criteria that a talented student from any background can meet is more fair than an informal system in which the talented poor are simply invisible.

## Conclusion

"Fairness" in education cannot mean giving every student the same instruction; it must mean giving every student instruction from which they can actually learn. The selective admissions theory tells us that performance-based placement converts family investment into demonstrated capability through a mechanism open to all. The average drag theory tells us that refusing to stratify does not protect the disadvantaged—it silently taxes our highest-potential students, and taxes most heavily those who cannot buy their way out of the average.

The burden of proof should now shift. We have decades of natural experiments in stratification, many badly designed, some quite good. What we lack is systematic, well-funded experimentation with the modern, permeable, subject-specific models described above. I call on districts, researchers, and funders to launch such trials at scale—with pre-registered outcomes, disaggregated results, and honest reporting of who gains and who loses. Efficiency without fairness is unworthy of public education. But fairness without efficiency strands the very students—brilliant, hungry, and under-resourced—whom public education most exists to lift.

---

*A note on this piece: as requested, this commentary is written in the persona of Dr. Jane Smith and argues one side of a genuinely contested empirical and normative debate. The strongest counterarguments—concerning early tracking's entrenchment of socioeconomic inequality, the asymmetry of peer effects, and measurement bias in admissions—deserve equal airtime, and readers should treat this as an advocacy piece rather than a neutral review of the evidence. I'm happy to also draft the opposing commentary or a balanced literature review if that would be useful.*
